title: Why Don't Crocodiles Eat Capybaras? The Real Answer
description: The internet thinks capybaras are friends with everyone, even crocodiles. Scientists say the truth is colder, and much more interesting. Plus four wild animal discoveries from the last few weeks, counting down to the real answer.
sources: Earth.com (12 Oct 2026) Capybaras share riverbanks with crocodiles, but the peace treaty is less friendly than it looks — https://www.earth.com/animals/capybaras-share-riverbanks-with-crocodiles-but-the-peace-treaty-is-less-friendly-than-it-looks

Cavalcanti S. & Gese E. (2010) Kill rates and predation patterns of jaguars in the southern Pantanal, Brazil. Journal of Mammalogy — https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1885&context=icwdm_usdanwrc
Earth.com (13 Oct 2026) Gannets slam into the sea at 70 mph, and their square neck bones take most of the hit — https://www.earth.com/animals/gannets-square-neck-vertebrae-plunge-dives

Los Angeles Times (19 Sep 2026) Meet Earth's newest wild cat species, the first named in over a century — https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-09-19/meet-earths-newest-wild-cat-species-first-named-in-over-century
Vaisvil B. et al. (2026) Epigenetic insights into extreme longevity in the world's oldest terrestrial animal, Jonathan. Science Advances — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adw8887

scenes.say: You've seen the photos. A capybara chilling right next to a crocodile. Totally calm.

scenes.label: The internet's theory
scenes.say: The internet says capybaras are so chill that even predators love them. It's a cute idea. It's also wrong.

scenes.label: Sitting ON caimans
scenes.say: Some photos even show capybaras sitting right on top of a caiman. Millions of people see that and think, wow, best friends.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the deal. We'll count down five wild animal discoveries from the last few weeks. And at number one, I'll show you what's really going on between capybaras and crocodiles.

scenes.label: Spoiler: it's not love
scenes.say: Spoiler. It isn't friendship. It's math. And there's a third animal in this story that scares both of them.

scenes.label: The internet's favorite
scenes.say: And honestly, it makes sense that we want it to be true. Capybaras have become one of the internet's favorite animals. The calm one that gets along with everybody. Here's why that picture is misleading.

scenes.label: The 70 mph dive
scenes.say: Number five. A bird that crashes into the ocean, headfirst, on purpose.

scenes.label: 100 feet up
scenes.say: Meet the northern gannet. It flies about thirty meters above the sea, spots a school of fish, and folds into a nosedive.

scenes.label: About 110 km/h
scenes.say: It hits the water at around seventy miles per hour. That's about a hundred and ten kilometers per hour. Every single time it hunts.

scenes.label: So why no broken neck?
scenes.say: So how does it not break its neck? That's exactly what scientists at the University of Washington wanted to know.

scenes.label: 15 neck bones
scenes.say: Because on paper, it should. A gannet's neck has fifteen vertebrae stacked in a slight S-curve. That sounds fragile for a bird that lands headfirst.

scenes.label: CT scans of skeletons
scenes.say: They scanned museum skeletons and found the answer in the bones. A gannet's neck vertebrae are short and almost square, which helps them take the hit.

scenes.label: Not shorter, squarer
scenes.say: And here's the surprise. Their necks aren't really shorter than their non-diving cousins, the cormorants. The bones are just squarer, so they handle bigger forces.

scenes.label: Muscles lock in
scenes.say: Earlier studies showed that neck muscles also lock everything in place right before impact. Bones plus muscle. A built-in crash helmet.

scenes.label: Kingfishers? Way slower
scenes.say: Other birds plunge-dive too, like kingfishers and terns. But they hit the water at about twenty two to twenty five miles per hour. The gannet family is in a league of its own.

scenes.label: Gannets and boobies
scenes.say: In fact, gannets and their cousins the boobies are the only seabird family that plunge-dives at those speeds. Every one of them does it.

scenes.label: A brand new cat
scenes.say: Number four. A new species of wild cat. The first one formally described since nineteen twenty three.

scenes.label: Meet the tilcayo
scenes.say: It's called the tilcayo. It lives in the cloud forests of Bolivia, and it's tiny. Smaller than a house cat, weighing around three pounds.

scenes.label: About 1.4 kilos
scenes.say: We're talking about forty six centimeters long and roughly one point four kilos. Spotted like a miniature leopard.

scenes.label: Hiding in plain sight
scenes.say: Here's the crazy part. People living there already knew this cat. Scientists just thought it was one of its look-alike relatives, the tiger cats.

scenes.label: DNA cracked it
scenes.say: It took DNA tests to prove the tilcayo is its own species. Which means a whole species of cat was hiding in plain sight, for over a century.

scenes.label: 1.4 million years apart
scenes.say: The genetic work suggests its lineage may have split off around one point four million years ago. So it's been its own thing for a very, very long time.

scenes.label: Once a pet
scenes.say: And the cat that helped scientists describe it? According to reports, he had once lived briefly as somebody's house pet.

scenes.label: 194 years old
scenes.say: Number three. An animal that was probably hatched before anyone had ever taken a photograph of a person.

scenes.label: Meet Jonathan
scenes.say: This is Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise. He's estimated to be about one hundred ninety four years old, the oldest known living land animal.

scenes.label: Arrived in 1882
scenes.say: He was already fully grown when he arrived on the island of Saint Helena in eighteen eighty two. He's outlived two world wars and almost everyone who has ever looked after him.

scenes.label: Older than Queen Victoria's reign
scenes.say: He was alive during the reign of King William the Fourth, before Queen Victoria even took the throne. Today he lives on the lawn of the governor's house.

scenes.label: Blind, still hungry
scenes.say: He's lost his sight to cataracts, but his keepers say he still eats well and stays active. Honestly, goals.

scenes.label: A cheek swab
scenes.say: This month, scientists published the first epigenetic study of Jonathan. Instead of taking blood, they gently swabbed his cheek.

scenes.label: Parts of him look 5
scenes.say: What they found is wild. His DNA shows plenty of normal aging. But some regions looked remarkably orderly, in some cases more like a five-year-old tortoise.

scenes.label: Cambridge + Vanderbilt
scenes.say: The team included researchers from the University of Cambridge and Vanderbilt University Medical Center. They compared him with four other Aldabra tortoises, from a five-year-old to older adults.

scenes.label: Just one tortoise
scenes.say: Now, careful. That's one animal compared with just four others. So it's a clue, not a secret to living forever. But what a clue.

scenes.label: The real boss
scenes.say: Number two. The animal that hunts crocodiles.

scenes.label: The Pantanal
scenes.say: This is the Pantanal in Brazil, one of the biggest wetlands on Earth. It's full of caimans, which are close relatives of alligators. And it's full of capybaras.

scenes.label: 10 jaguars, GPS collars
scenes.say: Researchers fitted ten jaguars here with GPS collars and checked their kill sites. They documented four hundred thirty eight prey items.

scenes.label: 24.4% were caimans
scenes.say: Guess what showed up a lot. Caimans. About twenty four percent of the kills. Second only to cattle.

scenes.label: Floods = caiman season
scenes.say: And it got more intense when the water rose. As floods spread the caimans across the landscape, jaguars killed even more of them. Female jaguars killed more caimans than males did.

scenes.label: Crocodile hunters
scenes.say: Think about that. The reptile everyone fears is regular dinner for a big cat. And in that study, capybaras were only about two percent of the kills.

scenes.label: Hold that thought
scenes.say: So the jaguar is the real boss of this riverbank. Hold that thought, because it matters for number one.

scenes.label: The truth
scenes.say: Number one. Why don't crocodiles eat capybaras?

scenes.label: Big. Heavy. Teeth.
scenes.say: First, size. An adult capybara is the biggest rodent in the world. It's heavy, muscular, and it has long, sharp front teeth.

scenes.label: Not worth the risk
scenes.say: For a caiman, grabbing one is a risky fight. A researcher quoted by Earth dot com put it simply. Adult capybaras just aren't worth the trouble and the injury.

scenes.label: Fish are easier
scenes.say: Second, menu. Caimans mostly eat fish and smaller prey. When there's plenty of easy food around, why wrestle a rodent that can weigh up to sixty kilos?

scenes.label: "I've seen them sleep together"
scenes.say: The same researcher said attacks on adults are rare, especially when there's plenty of fish. She's even seen the two species sleeping next to each other in the wild.

scenes.label: But the babies…
scenes.say: But here's the dark twist. The babies are a different story. Young capybaras are on the menu for caimans, and for foxes, ocelots, birds of prey and anacondas.

scenes.label: Anacondas too
scenes.say: And the green anaconda? It's one of the predators that takes young capybaras too. The riverbank is not a cozy place for a baby.

scenes.label: The huddle
scenes.say: So capybaras do something clever. When they're attacked on land, a group can form a huddle, babies in the middle, adults facing out.

scenes.label: Picking safe spots
scenes.say: Researchers also found that capybaras can lower their risk by choosing safer areas, and feeding longer when predators aren't nearby. They're not naive. They're calculating.

scenes.label: Same enemy
scenes.say: And remember the jaguar? It hunts both of them. So a calm capybara next to a caiman isn't friendship. It's two animals that both have bigger problems.

scenes.label: It's math, not love
scenes.say: An adult capybara resting by a caiman has the odds on its side. That's the real secret. Not friendship. Just math.

scenes.label: Ancient roots
scenes.say: And capybaras have deep roots in South America. Fossils of their extinct relatives have even turned up in the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth today. They've been surviving predators for a very long time.

scenes.label: Next time you see the meme
scenes.say: So next time you see that meme of a capybara relaxing beside a crocodile, you'll know the real story. It's not a hug. It's a cold calculation, and right now, it's working.

scenes.label: Which one got you?
scenes.say: So which one surprised you most? The seventy mile per hour bird, the hidden cat, the hundred ninety four year old tortoise, or the capybara truth? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Capybaras Aren't Friends With Crocodiles
short.description: Why caimans rarely attack adult capybaras: size, risk and easier food. Source: Earth.com, 12 Oct 2026.

scenes.say: You think capybaras are friends with crocodiles? They're not. Here's the truth.
An adult capybara is the world's biggest rodent. Up to sixty kilos of muscle, with long, sharp front teeth.
For a caiman, that's a risky fight. And they mostly eat fish, which is way easier.
But the babies? They're on the menu. For caimans, foxes, ocelots and even anacondas.
And jaguars hunt both of them. In one study, about a quarter of jaguar kills were caimans.
So that calm photo isn't love. It's math. Which means, no, capybaras are not friends with crocodiles.
